subject: psychology
topic: You miss what you are not looking for, even a gorilla
angle: Even experts can fail to see massive, obvious objects like gorillas if their attention is focused on a specific task, regardless of whether they are looking directly at the object.
title: The Filter of Attention

hooks.text: What are you missing right now?
You can look directly at an object and still not see it.
Your focus is making you blind to your own life.
A red cross moves across a screen for five seconds.

reveal.headline: You do not see what you are not looking for.
reveal.body: Eighty-three percent of radiologists did not see a gorilla that was 48 times the size of the average nodule. They looked directly at its location.

explain.headline: Your goals dictate your reality.
explain.body: Inattentional blindness increases with the perceptual load of your task. Your own attentional goals are the most influential factor in what you notice.

matters.headline: Your focus is a filter.
matters.body: That may be why you miss significant events in your life. When your mind is occupied, it filters out even the most salient information.

example.headline: A familiar walk.
example.body: You walk through a crowded station with your headphones on. You focus on your destination. You pass a person in distress and do not see them.

question.headline: What is happening right now that you are missing?

claims.text: Eighty-three percent of radiologists did not see a gorilla that was 48 times the size of the average nodule.
claims.quote: A gorilla, 48 times the size of the average nodule, was inserted in the last case that was presented. Eighty-three percent of the radiologists did not see the gorilla.

claims.text: The majority of radiologists who missed the gorilla looked directly at its location.
claims.quote: Eye tracking revealed that the majority of those who missed the gorilla looked directly at its location.

claims.text: When attending to black items or white items in a dynamic display, nearly 30% of observers failed to notice a bright red cross move across the display, even though it had a unique color, luminance, shape, and motion trajectory and was visible for 5s.
claims.quote: when attending to black items or white items in a dynamic display, nearly 30% of observers failed to notice a bright red cross move across the display, even though it had a unique color, luminance, shape, and motion trajectory and was visible for 5s.

claims.text: Doubling or even tripling the time when the unexpected object was visible barely affected the likelihood of noticing it.
claims.quote: Doubling or even tripling the time when the unexpected object was visible barely affected the likelihood of noticing it and had no impact on how accurately subjects reported its features.

claims.text: Inattentional blindness significantly increases with the perceptual load of the task.
claims.quote: The results reveal that, in line with the perceptual account of the Load Theory, inattentional blindness significantly increases with the perceptual load of the task.

claims.text: The most influential factor affecting noticing is a person's own attentional goals.
claims.quote: Although some stimulus properties can influence noticing of unexpected objects, the most influential factor affecting noticing is a person's own attentional goals.

verdict: The evidence shows that inattentional blindness is a robust phenomenon where specific attentional goals and perceptual loads can cause people to miss highly salient, visible events.
caveat: The cognitive account of the Load Theory is not clearly supported by the empirical findings analyzed in the meta-analysis.
caption:
Your brain filters out the world based on your current goals.

Research shows that high perceptual loads and specific goals can cause people to miss highly salient events. However, the cognitive account of the Load Theory is not clearly supported by the empirical findings analyzed in a meta-analysis.

What is your current goal preventing you from seeing?
